identification.summary: China-origin espionage actor that Microsoft tracks as Checkered Typhoon (formerly CHLORINE), mapping to it the vendor names DEEP PANDA, APT19, ATG50, TG-3551 and Red Gargoyle [S1]. Under the Deep Panda name, CrowdStrike reported intrusions into US national security think tanks in 2014 and a campaign against defense, healthcare, government and technology organizations using Sakula malware [S2][S3]. Security firms including CrowdStrike, RSA and ThreatConnect linked Deep Panda to the 2014-2015 Anthem and OPM breaches [S5]. Under the APT19 name, FireEye reported a 2017 phishing campaign against law and investment firms [S7]. Fortinet tied Deep Panda to 2022 Log4Shell exploitation of VMware Horizon servers [S10].
identification.firstObserved: Public reporting under the Deep Panda name dates to July 2014 [S2]. Symantec says Black Vine, a cluster press links to the Anthem breach, has been active since at least 2012 [S6]; Microsoft does not list Black Vine in its mapping [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Checkered Typhoon (formerly CHLORINE); 'Typhoon' denotes China origin in Microsoft's taxonomy [S1]. Microsoft's mapping lists only CHLORINE, DEEP PANDA, ATG50, APT19, TG-3551 and Red Gargoyle as other names [S1]. Other aliases in this record (Black Vine, Codoso/C0d0so0, Shell Crew, KungFu Kittens, PinkPanther, WebMasters, Sunshop Group, etc.) come from MISP/MITRE imports and are not confirmed by Microsoft; MITRE tracks Deep Panda (G0009) and APT19 (G0073) as separate group entries. The Forbes.com watering hole was attributed by iSIGHT and Invincea to 'Codoso Team', not by Microsoft [S4]. Sakula is described by CrowdStrike as a limited-release tool used by several adversaries, so Sakula use alone does not identify this actor [S3].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China (Microsoft assigns the actor to its China-origin 'Typhoon' family) [S1]. FireEye assesses APT19 is composed of freelancers with some degree of sponsorship by the Chinese government [S7]. CrowdStrike said in 2014 it believed Deep Panda works for or is funded by the Chinese government [S2].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft attributes the actor to China by family assignment but publishes no confidence level in its mapping [S1]. CrowdStrike's Dmitri Alperovitch expressed 'great confidence' the actors were state-sponsored (2014) [S2]. Researchers told Reuters in 2015 the group's exact affiliation with the Chinese government was not known and it might be a private contractor [S5]. The 2019 US indictment over the Anthem breach does not allege Chinese government involvement [S9]. China has denied involvement [S5].
attribution.basis: Vendor telemetry and malware analysis (CrowdStrike, FireEye, Fortinet, Symantec, ThreatConnect) [S2][S3][S5][S6][S7][S10]; shared tooling and stolen code-signing certificates across the OPM and Anthem intrusions [S5]; US criminal cases against Yu Pingan (Sakula supplier, 2017) and Fujie Wang (Anthem, 2019) [S8][S9].

objectives: Espionage against foreign-policy and national security research organizations, including rapid re-tasking to Iraq and Middle East experts in June 2014 [S2]; theft of large personal-data holdings from health insurers and, per vendor and press reporting, the US Office of Personnel Management [S5][S9]; and theft of data from law and investment firms for competitive economic purposes [S7].

sectors: National security and foreign-policy think tanks [S2]
Financial, academic, cosmetics and travel (2022 opportunistic Log4Shell activity) [S10]
targeting.notes: Targeting has shifted with events: CrowdStrike observed a sharp move from Asia-focused think-tank experts to Iraq experts on 18 June 2014 [S2]. The 2022 Log4Shell activity was opportunistic rather than sector-specific [S10].

capabilities.summary: Initial access through spear-phishing (RTF exploiting CVE-2017-0199, macro-enabled Excel documents, regsvr32 'Squiblydoo' whitelisting bypass) [S7][S9], drive-by exploits [S2], strategic web compromise (Forbes.com, attributed to Codoso) [S4], and exploitation of public-facing services (Log4Shell on VMware Horizon) [S10]. Tooling includes Sakula disguised as Adobe Reader and Juniper VPN installers and loaded by DLL side-loading [S3], Cobalt Strike BEACON [S7], Mivast (Black Vine reporting) [S6], the Milestone backdoor and the Fire Chili kernel rootkit [S10]. The actor repeatedly uses code-signing certificates stolen from Korean and US software and game companies [S3][S5][S10], and look-alike credential-harvesting domains such as We11point.com and OPM-Learning.org [S5].

campaigns.name: Anthem breach
campaigns.summary: Intrusions starting February 2014 led to theft of data on about 78.8 million people; Symantec linked it to Black Vine and Mivast, vendors to Deep Panda, and DOJ indicted Fujie Wang in 2019.

campaigns.name: Think-tank intrusions and Iraq re-tasking
campaigns.summary: CrowdStrike reported Deep Panda compromises of several US national security think tanks and a shift on 18 June 2014 to targeting Iraq and Middle East experts.

campaigns.name: 'Ironman' Sakula campaign
campaigns.summary: CrowdStrike reported Deep Panda use of signed Sakula variants against defense, healthcare, government and technology organizations.

campaigns.name: Forbes.com watering hole (Codoso)
campaigns.summary: A Forbes.com widget was compromised 28 Nov to 1 Dec 2014 to serve Flash and IE zero-days; iSIGHT and Invincea attributed it to Codoso Team (an alias not in Microsoft's mapping).

campaigns.name: OPM breach linkage
campaigns.summary: CrowdStrike, RSA, ThreatConnect and others told Reuters they believed Deep Panda was behind both the OPM and Anthem breaches, citing shared Sakula use and a stolen DTOPTOOLZ certificate.

campaigns.name: APT19 law and investment firm phishing
campaigns.summary: FireEye observed phishing against at least seven global law and investment firms in May-June 2017, delivering Cobalt Strike BEACON.

campaigns.name: Arrest of Sakula supplier Yu Pingan
campaigns.summary: The FBI arrested Yu Pingan, alleged to have supplied malware including Sakula used against US companies from 2011 to 2014.

campaigns.name: Log4Shell / Fire Chili
campaigns.summary: Fortinet linked Log4Shell exploitation of VMware Horizon servers, the Milestone backdoor and the signed Fire Chili rootkit to Deep Panda.

diamond.adversary: PRC-attributed operators that Microsoft tracks as Checkered Typhoon [S1]; FireEye assesses APT19 is freelancers with some Chinese government sponsorship [S7]; individuals charged include Fujie Wang (Anthem) and malware supplier Yu Pingan [S8][S9].
diamond.capability: Sakula, Mivast, Cobalt Strike BEACON, Milestone backdoor, Fire Chili rootkit; Office exploits, macros, Log4Shell; stolen code-signing certificates [S3][S6][S7][S10].
diamond.infrastructure: Look-alike phishing and credential-harvest domains (We11point.com, OPM-Learning.org) [S5]; 2bunny[.]com and cloudsend[.]net domains for 2017 phishing and C2 [S7]; compromised legitimate websites used as watering holes [S4].
diamond.victim: US think tanks, defense contractors, health insurers, government personnel records, technology firms, and law and investment firms [S2][S3][S5][S7].
diamond.socioPolitical: Foreign-policy intelligence tied to world events (Iraq crisis 2014) [S2]; bulk personal data on US persons and federal employees [S5][S9]; competitive economic intelligence from law and investment firms [S7].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints, Microsoft Office, Internet Explorer/Flash, internet-facing VMware Horizon servers [S4][S7][S10].

gaps: Microsoft has published no actor profile, blog or confidence statement for Checkered Typhoon found in this research; the only Microsoft source is its name-mapping file [S1].

Cluster boundaries are unresolved: MITRE keeps Deep Panda (G0009) and APT19 (G0073) as separate groups, and Microsoft's mapping omits Black Vine, Codoso and Shell Crew, which press reporting associates with the Anthem and Forbes activity [S1][S4][S6].

The US government has not formally attributed OPM to this actor; the OPM link comes from vendor statements to Reuters and anonymous sources [S5]. The Anthem indictment does not allege PRC government involvement [S9].

Primary documents were not opened: CrowdStrike blogs (fetch blocked), Symantec's Black Vine white paper, Fortinet's Fire Chili blog, DOJ press releases and complaints (justice.gov blocked), and MITRE ATT&CK pages (fetch failed). Facts from them rely on press coverage.
The DOJ Anthem indictment date (2019-05) and the CrowdStrike Ironman date (2014-11) come from search-result coverage, not the opened documents.
No public reporting after 2022 attributed to Checkered Typhoon, Deep Panda or APT19 was found; current activity is unknown.
Fortinet noted overlaps between the 2022 activity and the Winnti group (shared stolen certificates and possibly C2) whose nature is unclear [S10].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Key terrain includes HR and personnel-records systems, health-benefit provider networks, cleared defense contractors, policy research partners, and internet-facing remote-access servers such as VMware Horizon [S3][S5][S10]. STEP 2 (effects): Theft of personnel and health records gives an adversary long-term targeting data on service members and cleared personnel; quick uptake of public exploits (Log4Shell) shrinks patch windows [S5][S9][S10]. STEP 3 (adversary template): Spear-phishing or exploitation of public-facing services, then signed implants (Sakula, BEACON, Milestone) loaded via side-loading or regsvr32, then rootkit concealment and data theft [S3][S7][S10]. STEP 4: MLCOA is quiet collection of policy and personal data from think tanks, contractors and benefit providers, re-tasked to world events [S2][S5]. MDCOA is bulk theft of DoD-adjacent personnel or medical data enabling targeting of cleared personnel. Candidate indicators: look-alike domains imitating benefit providers or OPM; binaries signed with stolen game- or software-company certificates; regsvr32 calling remote scrobj.dll scriptlets; PowerShell spawned from VMware Horizon/Tomcat processes; unknown kernel drivers [S5][S7][S10].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: include contractor and benefit-provider breaches in the common picture, since this actor's largest known thefts were outside government networks [S5][S9]. (2) Authorities: much victim data sits with private healthcare and legal firms, so response depends on law enforcement and partner reporting rather than DoD authorities [S7][S9]. (3) Mission assurance: personnel-data compromise is a lasting risk to force protection and counterintelligence; plan for long-tail impacts, not just remediation [S5]. (4) Coordination: work with DC3/DIB CS and FBI on stolen code-signing certificates and shared tooling that cross actor boundaries (Sakula, Winnti overlap) [S3][S10].
